newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Court annuls opposition victory in Belgrade.
newsitem.headline: Court annuls opposition victory in Belgrade.

text.p: Authorities on Sunday annulled an opposition election victory in the Serbian capital Belgrade, provoking a pledge of new protests by opponents of the ruling Socialists and President Slobodan Milosevic.
Leaders of the three-party opposition coalition said the decision showed the Socialists led by Milosevic were making a mockery of the democratic process.
"This is proof that power cannot be won in Serbia by elections, that power is won by robbery," Zoran Djindjic, one of the Zajedno (Together) coalition leaders, told Reuters.

"We have now been brought to a dramatic situation in which all citizens are becoming aware that the regime in Serbia cannot be changed by elections and cannot be changed legally but only in another way -- illegally, by uprisings, strikes, violence."
State television reported a municipal court ruling on Sunday which stripped Zajedno of a majority in the 110-seat city council, forcing another round of voting.
Electoral authorities had confirmed last Tuesday Zajedno had obtained 60 seats in Belgrade.
Courts and electoral commissions had already cancelled opposition victories in the largest towns, citing alleged irregularities.

The opposition, accusing the authorities of massive fraud, organised peaceful demonstrations in Belgrade and other towns over the past five days in the country's biggest street protests in three years.
The outcome of the local elections shocked the Socialists and has sparked a confrontation between the opposition and Milosevic, who has ruled Serbia with supreme authority for nine years.
The opposition says the local poll has punctured Milosevic's aura of invincibility but the court ruling in Belgrade raised the stakes in the standoff.
With Milosevic controlling a big police force and the state media, the opposition said it would try to exert pressure through strikes and civil disobedience.
University student leaders said they were planning a strike on Monday in support of the opposition at faculties in Belgrade as well in Nis, Kragujevac and Novi Sad.
Some 20,000 supporters in Belgrade braved rain and a light snowfall on Sunday afternoon in a demonstration scheduled before the court's decision was announced.
State television, Milosevic's main propaganda tool, said a "handful" of people attended the protest and portrayed the opposition as outlaws bent on violence.
"In the name of democracy, they are only using threats, force and violence," the television said.
Zajedno leaders have appealed for international support, which they said could tip the balance in their favour.
But Western countries have so far offered only muted statements expressing concern over possible election fraud.

The United States and European powers once accused Milosevic of igniting four years of war in former Yugoslavia. But they now view him as a guarantor of peace after he signed a U.S.-brokered peace treaty last year.
Senior American and European diplomats on Saturday met Yugoslav foreign minister Milan Milutinovic to discuss the situation but declined to discuss details of the talks.
Local media reported Milutinovic would travel to Brussels on Monday to meet European Union representatives.
After annulling results, electoral authorities have announced another round of voting on Wednesday or Sunday in various towns where the opposition has claimed victory.
Opposition leaders said they refused to participate in the next round which they called a farce.
